🆔 Introduction and requirements

Hinglish samajh: Har row ko ek ID chahiye. Ek database mein auto_increment chalta hai, par distributed system mein kai databases ek jaise numbers bana dete hain. Isliye hum aisa unique ID generator banate hain jiske IDs unique hon, numeric hon, 64 bit mein aayein, samay ke saath badhein (date se sort ho saken) aur jo 10,000 se zyada IDs per second bana sake. Chaar tareeke dekhenge: multi-master replication, UUID, ticket server aur Twitter Snowflake.

Every row in a database needs an ID that identifies it: an order number, a user id, a post id. On a single database server the easy answer is the auto_increment column: the database hands out 1, 2, 3, and so on. This stops working in a distributed system. A single database may not be big enough, and having many databases generate IDs with auto_increment means they will produce the same numbers, with high latency if they try to coordinate.

So this chapter designs a unique ID generator for a distributed system. The requirements are: IDs must be unique; IDs are numerical values that fit in 64 bits; IDs increase with time (they are ordered by date) but not necessarily by exactly +1; IDs should be sortable by date; and the system must handle high throughput: more than 10,000 IDs per second.

Notice a useful detail: "increase with time but not by +1" and "sortable by date" together mean that if you create item A before item B, A's ID is smaller than B's ID. That makes it easy to sort rows by ID instead of storing and sorting another timestamp. Over the next lessons we compare four approaches: multi-master replication, UUID, a ticket server and Twitter's Snowflake.

Requirements at a glance

RequirementValue
UniquenessNo two IDs are the same
TypeNumeric
SizeFits in 64 bits
OrderingIncreases with time (sortable by date), but not necessarily by +1
ThroughputMore than 10,000 IDs per second

✨ Features

  • IDs are unique, numeric and fit in 64 bits.
  • IDs are ordered by time, so they can be sorted by date.
  • The generator must make over 10,000 IDs per second.

✅ Benefits

  • A single numeric key that identifies a row.
  • Sorting by ID gives creation order.
  • Servers can create IDs independently, so there is no bottleneck.

⚠️ Problems

  • auto_increment does not work across many databases.
  • Clocks on different servers are never perfectly the same.
  • IDs must be generated very fast and with no single point of failure.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · Introduction + Step 1: Understanding the Problem

This chapter addresses the challenge of designing a unique ID generator for distributed systems. Traditional auto-increment keys are unsuitable in distributed environments due to scalability and synchronization challenges. The focus is on creating unique, sortable, 64-bit numerical IDs that meet the following requirements:

  • IDs must be unique and ordered by date.
  • IDs must fit within 64 bits.
  • The system should generate over 10,000 IDs per second.

Basic Requirements

  • IDs must be unique and numerical and should fit in 64 bits.
  • IDs increment with time but not strictly by +1.
  • IDs should be sortable by date.
  • System must handle high throughput (10,000 IDs/sec).

Interview questions and answers

Why can we not use auto_increment in a distributed system?
A single database cannot serve huge traffic, and several databases would each generate the same numbers. Coordinating them adds latency and complexity.
What are the requirements of the ID generator?
Unique, numeric, 64-bit, ordered by date and generated at more than 10,000 per second.
Cross question: Why must IDs be sortable by time?
So you can sort by ID instead of keeping and sorting another timestamp column. It also helps range queries and pagination.
Cross question: Why only 64 bits?
A 64-bit number fits a standard integer type, indexes efficiently and saves storage compared with a 128-bit ID.

🔁 Approach 1: Multi-master replication

Hinglish samajh: Pehla tareeka: database ka auto_increment hi use karo, par har baar 1 ki jagah k se badhao, jahan k database servers ki sankhya hai. Do servers ho to ek 1, 3, 5, 7 banata hai aur doosra 2, 4, 6, 8. Aasan hai, par kai nuksan hain: kai data centers mein scale karna mushkil, IDs samay ke order mein nahi rehte, aur server jodna ya hatana mushkil hai.

The first idea is to keep using the database's auto_increment, but change the step. Instead of increasing the ID by 1, each database increases it by k, where k is the number of database servers. With two servers, server 1 produces 1, 3, 5, 7 and server 2 produces 2, 4, 6, 8. The IDs are different on each server, and each server can generate IDs on its own.

This approach is easy to build because it uses a built-in database feature, and it scales in terms of IDs per second as you add servers. But the notes list several drawbacks. It is hard to scale across multiple data centers. The IDs do not go up with time across servers: server 1 may be at 1,001 while server 2 is only at 700, so a newer item can have a smaller ID. And it does not handle adding or removing servers well, because changing k breaks the numbering scheme.

Two servers with a step of 2

Time order of requestsServerID generated
1stServer 11
2ndServer 22
3rdServer 13
4thServer 15
5thServer 24

✨ Features

  • Each database increases IDs by k (the number of servers).
  • Uses a standard database feature.
  • IDs are numeric and unique.

✅ Benefits

  • Simple, no new software.
  • More servers give more throughput.
  • Numeric IDs.

⚠️ Problems

  • Hard to scale across data centers.
  • IDs do not always increase with time.
  • Poor fit when servers are added or removed.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · 1. Multi-Master Replication

  • Approach: Use database auto_increment with step increments (e.g., +k for k servers).
  • Drawbacks:
    • Hard to scale across data centers.
    • IDs do not always increase with time.
    • Scaling issues when servers are added/removed.

Interview questions and answers

How does multi-master replication generate unique IDs?
Each database server increments its ID by k (the number of servers), starting at a different offset, so the servers never produce the same number.
What are its drawbacks?
It is hard to scale across data centers, IDs do not follow time order across servers, and adding or removing servers is awkward.
Cross question: Does it meet the sortable by date requirement?
No. Two servers advance at different speeds, so a later item can get a smaller ID than an earlier one.
Cross question: When is it acceptable?
For a small system with a fixed number of servers where strict time ordering is not needed.

🧬 Approach 2: UUID

Hinglish samajh: UUID ek 128 bit ka number hai jo har web server khud bana sakta hai, aur do UUIDs ke takrane ki sambhavna na ke barabar hai. Isme koi coordination nahi chahiye aur koi single point of failure nahi. Par UUID 64 bit se bada hai, time ke hisaab se sort nahi hota aur numeric nahi bhi ho sakta, isliye hamari requirements poori nahi hoti.

A UUID (Universally Unique Identifier) is a 128-bit number that is generated by the computer itself and looks like 09c93e62-50b4-468d-bf8a-c07e1040bfb2. The chance that two UUIDs collide is extremely small (you would have to generate billions of IDs every second for many years before a collision becomes likely). So every web server can create UUIDs independently without talking to any other server or database.

In this design each web server has an ID generator, and requests go straight to it. There is no coordination, no single point of failure, and it scales as easily as adding more web servers. These are real advantages.

But UUIDs fail two requirements. They are 128 bits long, which is more than our 64-bit limit. And they are not sortable by time and may not be numeric (they contain letters). This also makes them less efficient as database primary keys, because random IDs insert into random places in an index. Some newer UUID versions (such as time-ordered UUIDs) improve sorting, but they are still 128 bits.

✨ Features

  • 128-bit identifier generated locally.
  • No coordination between servers.
  • Very low chance of collision.

✅ Benefits

  • Simple to use and available in every language.
  • No single point of failure.
  • Scales easily with the number of web servers.

⚠️ Problems

  • Exceeds the 64-bit requirement.
  • Not sortable by time and may be non-numeric.
  • Random values make database indexes less efficient.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · 2. UUID (Universally Unique Identifier)

  • Approach:
    • Generate 128-bit unique identifiers independently on each server using UUID.
    • UUIDs can be generated independently without coordination between servers
  • Advantages:
    • No coordination needed between servers.
    • Scales easily with web servers.
  • Drawbacks:
    • Exceeds 64-bit requirement.
    • IDs are not sortable by time and may be non-numeric.

Interview questions and answers

What is a UUID?
A 128-bit universally unique identifier that each server can generate on its own, with a negligible chance of duplicates.
Why is a UUID not suitable here?
It is 128 bits (more than 64), it is not time sortable and may not be numeric.
Cross question: How likely is a UUID collision?
Extremely unlikely for random UUIDs. You would need to generate an astronomical number of them before a duplicate becomes probable.
Cross question: When is a UUID a good choice anyway?
When you do not need ordering or small size, for example for public tokens, request ids or keys created on offline devices.

🎫 Approach 3: Ticket server

Hinglish samajh: Ticket server ek kendriya (centralized) idea hai: ek database server mein auto_increment wali table hoti hai aur har web server ID maangne par uske paas jaata hai (Flickr ne isse use kiya). Fayde: numeric IDs aur chhote systems ke liye aasan. Nuksan: ye single point of failure hai, aur zyada ticket servers lagane par synchronization ki dikkat aati hai.

A ticket server is a simple, centralized idea. One database server (the ticket server) has a table with an auto_increment column. Whenever any web server needs an ID, it asks the ticket server, which returns the next number. This idea was famously used by Flickr.

It has clear advantages: the IDs are numeric, it is very simple to build for a small or medium system, and it uses a standard database feature. All IDs come from one place, so they are unique and roughly in time order.

The drawbacks come from the centralization. The ticket server is a single point of failure: if it goes down, all the servers that need IDs are stuck. You can add more ticket servers to avoid this, but then you face synchronization problems (the same issues as multi-master) and more complexity. Also every ID creation is a network call, which adds latency at high volumes.

✨ Features

  • One central server with an auto_increment counter.
  • Web servers request IDs from it.
  • Used in practice by Flickr.

✅ Benefits

  • Numeric IDs.
  • Easy to build for small and medium systems.
  • IDs are in order.

⚠️ Problems

  • Single point of failure.
  • Synchronization challenges with several ticket servers.
  • Every ID needs a network round trip, which limits throughput.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · 3. Ticket Server

  • Approach: Use a centralized database server to increment and assign IDs.
  • Advantages:
    • Simple to implement for small-scale systems.
    • Generates numeric IDs.
  • Drawbacks:
    • Single point of failure.
    • Synchronization challenges in multi-server setups.

Interview questions and answers

How does a ticket server work?
One database with an auto_increment column hands out the next number each time a web server asks for an ID.
What is the main weakness?
It is a single point of failure, and scaling it with more ticket servers brings synchronization problems.
Cross question: How would you reduce the risk?
Run two or more ticket servers (for example one issues odd, the other even IDs) with failover, or have web servers fetch IDs in blocks to reduce calls. These add complexity.
Cross question: Would you pick a ticket server for a global system?
Probably not. A decentralized design such as Snowflake avoids the single point of failure and the network round trips.

❄️ Approach 4: Twitter Snowflake

Hinglish samajh: Snowflake mein 64 bit ke ID ko hisson mein baanta jaata hai: 1 sign bit (hamesha 0), 41 bit timestamp (custom epoch se milliseconds), 5 bit datacenter ID (32 data centers), 5 bit machine ID (32 machines) aur 12 bit sequence number (ek millisecond mein 4096 IDs tak). Timestamp sabse upar hone se IDs time ke hisaab se sort hote hain. Isme koi central server nahi hota, isliye single point of failure nahi. Zaroori: clocks synchronized hon (NTP).

The approach we choose is Twitter Snowflake. The idea is: instead of generating an ID in one piece, divide a 64-bit ID into sections, so that different servers can never produce the same value and the time is built into the number. There is no central server and no coordination: every machine generates IDs on its own.

The 64 bits are split like this. Sign bit (1 bit): always 0, reserved for the future (it can tell signed from unsigned numbers). Timestamp (41 bits): the number of milliseconds since a custom starting time called the epoch. Twitter's epoch is 1288834974657, which is November 4, 2010, 01:42:54 UTC. Because the timestamp is in the highest bits, IDs sort by time. Datacenter ID (5 bits): up to 2^5 = 32 data centers. Machine ID (5 bits): up to 32 machines per data center. Sequence number (12 bits): for each ID created on a machine in the same millisecond, the sequence is increased; it supports up to 2^12 = 4,096 IDs per millisecond and resets to 0 every millisecond.

The advantages: it scales (10,000+ IDs per second per cluster is easy; one machine alone can make up to 4,096,000 per second in theory), IDs are time-ordered, and it is decentralized, so there is no single point of failure. Another nice fact: with 41 bits of milliseconds, the timestamp lasts about 69.7 years from the epoch, which is plenty for most systems.

The 64-bit Snowflake layout

SectionBitsPosition (from the right)MeaningCapacity
Sign1bit 63Always 0-
Timestamp41bits 22 to 62Milliseconds since the custom epochabout 69.7 years
Datacenter ID5bits 17 to 21Which data center32 data centers
Machine ID5bits 12 to 16Which machine in the data center32 machines each
Sequence number12bits 0 to 11Counter within one millisecond on one machine4,096 IDs per millisecond

Worked example (my numbers)

PartValueShifted value
Timestamp (ms since epoch)1,0001,000 << 22 = 4,194,304,000
Datacenter ID11 << 17 = 131,072
Machine ID22 << 12 = 8,192
Sequence number55
Final ID (sum of the parts)4,194,443,269

A simple Snowflake generator (C#)

public class Snowflake
{
    const long Epoch = 1288834974657L;          ␀class="nu">0␀
    const int  DcBits = class="nu">5, MachineBits = class="nu">5, SeqBits = class="nu">12;
    const long MaxSeq = (1L << SeqBits) - class="nu">1;     ␀class="nu">1␀

    readonly long dc, machine;
    long lastMs = -class="nu">1, seq = class="nu">0;

    public Snowflake(long datacenterId, long machineId) { dc = datacenterId; machine = machineId; }

    public long NextId()
    {
        lock (this)
        {
            long now = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.ToUnixTimeMilliseconds();
            if (now < lastMs) throw new Exception(␀class="nu">9␀);

            if (now == lastMs)
            {
                seq = (seq + class="nu">1) & MaxSeq;                    ␀class="nu">2␀
                if (seq == class="nu">0) while ((now = Now()) <= lastMs) { }   ␀class="nu">3␀
            }
            else seq = class="nu">0;                                    ␀class="nu">4␀

            lastMs = now;
            return ((now - Epoch) << (DcBits + MachineBits + SeqBits))   ␀class="nu">5␀
                 | (dc      << (MachineBits + SeqBits))                 ␀class="nu">6␀
                 | (machine << SeqBits)                                 ␀class="nu">7␀
                 | seq;                                                 ␀class="nu">8␀
        }
    }
    static long Now() => DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.ToUnixTimeMilliseconds();
}

✨ Features

  • 64 bits split into sign, timestamp, datacenter, machine and sequence.
  • Fully decentralized: every machine makes IDs on its own.
  • IDs are sortable by time.

✅ Benefits

  • Scalable: handles 10,000+ IDs per second across many servers.
  • Time-ordered: sorting by ID gives creation order.
  • Decentralized: no single point of failure.

⚠️ Problems

  • It depends on synchronized clocks across servers.
  • The datacenter and machine IDs must be assigned without clashes.
  • If the clock moves backwards, the generator must wait or fail.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · 4. Twitter Snowflake Approach

  • Approach:
  • Divide IDs into sections to ensure uniqueness and scalability.
  • Sign Bit (1 bit): Always 0, potentially distinguishing signed and unsigned numbers.
  • Timestamp (41 bits): Milliseconds since a custom epoch (Twitter's default is 1288834974657, equivalent to Nov 04, 2010, 01:42:54 UTC). Ensures IDs are time-ordered.
  • Datacenter ID (5 bits): Identifies up to 2^5 = 32 datacenters.
  • Machine ID (5 bits): Identifies up to 2^5 = 32 machines within each datacenter.
  • Sequence Number (12 bits): Tracks IDs generated on a machine within the same millisecond, supporting up to 2^12 = 4096 IDs per millisecond. The sequence resets to 0 every millisecond.
  • Advantages:
    • Scalability: Handles 10,000+ IDs per second across multiple servers.
    • Time-Order: Ensures IDs are sortable by time.
    • Decentralization: No single point of failure.

Interview questions and answers

Explain the Snowflake ID structure.
1 sign bit (always 0), 41 bits of timestamp in milliseconds since a custom epoch, 5 bits datacenter ID, 5 bits machine ID and 12 bits of sequence number, totaling 64 bits.
How many IDs can it create per millisecond and per second?
Each machine can create up to 2^12 = 4,096 IDs per millisecond, which is about 4 million per second per machine, far above 10,000 per second.
Why is the timestamp in the most significant bits?
So that IDs sort by time: a larger timestamp always gives a larger number regardless of the lower bits.
Cross question: What happens when the clock moves backwards?
The generator may produce duplicate or out-of-order IDs, so a safe implementation refuses to issue IDs (or waits) until the clock catches up. Use NTP to limit drift.
Cross question: How long does a 41-bit timestamp last?
2^41 milliseconds, which is about 69.7 years from the epoch.

🔧 Additional considerations: clocks, tuning and high availability

Hinglish samajh: Snowflake mein teen baatein dhyan mein rakhni hain. Pehli: clock synchronization, jiske liye NTP use hota hai aur clock peeche jaye to generator ko ID banana rok dena chahiye. Doosri: section length tuning, yaani bits ka batwara zaroorat ke hisaab se badla ja sakta hai (jaise kam sequence bits aur zyada timestamp bits). Teesri: high availability, kyunki ID generator mission-critical hai, isliye redundancy aur failover rakhein.

Snowflake works well, but there are three practical points to handle. The first is clock synchronization. The design assumes that all ID generators have the same clock. This can fail when a machine runs on many cores or when machines are in different data centers. The standard solution is the Network Time Protocol (NTP), which keeps clocks of different machines close to each other. A good generator also detects when its clock goes backwards and refuses to create IDs until it recovers.

The second is section length tuning. The split of 41, 5, 5 and 12 bits is not sacred. You can change it to fit your use. For example, a system with low concurrency but a long life may need fewer sequence bits and more timestamp bits. A system with many machines may need more machine bits.

The third is high availability. An ID generator is a mission-critical component: if it fails, nothing can be created. So build it with redundancy and failover, for example run several generators per data center and let clients fall back to another one if the first does not respond.

Considerations and responses

ConcernWhy it mattersWhat to do
Clock synchronizationDifferent clocks can create duplicate or unordered IDsUse NTP; detect backward clock jumps
Section length tuningThe right split depends on concurrency and system lifetimeAdjust bits (for example fewer sequence bits, more timestamp bits)
High availabilityThe generator is critical; failure blocks all writesRedundancy, several generators, failover

✨ Features

  • NTP for clock synchronization.
  • Adjustable bit sizes.
  • Redundancy and failover.

✅ Benefits

  • Fewer duplicate or out-of-order IDs.
  • The design fits different workloads.
  • The service keeps running when a node fails.

⚠️ Problems

  • Perfect clock sync is impossible; there is always a small drift.
  • Changing bit sizes later is hard because existing IDs have the old layout.
  • Redundancy means more machines to run.

Original notes from the repository

Source: liquidslr/system-design-notes · 1. Clock Synchronization + 2. Section Length Tuning + 3. High Availability

  • Challenge: ID generation assumes synchronized clocks across servers.
  • Solution: Use Network Time Protocol (NTP) to minimize drift.
  • Adjust section sizes (e.g., fewer sequence bits, more timestamp bits) based on use case.
  • ID generators are mission-critical and must be fault-tolerant.
  • Consider redundancy and failover mechanisms.

Interview questions and answers

What clock problems can affect Snowflake IDs?
Different machines can have slightly different clocks, and a clock can jump backwards. That can give duplicates or unordered IDs. Use NTP and refuse to issue IDs when the clock goes back.
How would you tune the bit sections?
Fewer sequence bits and more timestamp bits if there is little concurrency and the system must last long. More machine bits if you have many generator machines.
Cross question: How do you give each machine a unique machine ID?
Assign them through configuration or a coordination service such as ZooKeeper, so that no two generators share the same datacenter and machine pair.
Why must the ID generator be highly available?
Because it is mission critical: if it is down, the system cannot create new records.

⚖️ Comparing the four approaches

Hinglish samajh: Chaaron tareekon ki tulna: multi-master time order mein nahi aur scale karna mushkil; UUID bahut lamba aur sort nahi hota; ticket server single point of failure hai; Snowflake saari requirements poori karta hai (unique, 64 bit, time se sortable, decentralized, tez) par synchronized clocks maangta hai. Interview mein sirf jeetne wala hi nahi, balki baaki kyon haare ye bhi samjhao. Ye comparison table meri taraf se ek saar hai.

Let us put everything in one table. The point of a comparison in an interview is not just to name the winner but to show you understand why the others lose. (This summary table is my own, based on the notes.)

Multi-master replication is easy but not time-ordered and hard to scale. UUID is easy and decentralized but too long and not sortable. A ticket server is simple and ordered but a single point of failure. Snowflake meets all the requirements but needs good clocks and a way to assign machine IDs. For the requirements in this chapter (64-bit, time-sortable, more than 10,000 per second), Snowflake is the best fit.

Approach comparison

ApproachUniqueFits 64 bitsTime sortableSingle point of failureMain drawback
Multi-master replicationYesYesNoNoHard to scale across data centers, not time ordered
UUIDYesNo (128 bits)NoNoToo long, not numeric or sortable
Ticket serverYesYesRoughlyYesSingle point of failure, synchronization issues
Twitter SnowflakeYesYesYesNoNeeds synchronized clocks

✨ Features

  • Four approaches compared on the same criteria.
  • Snowflake meets every requirement.
  • Each other approach fails at least one.

✅ Benefits

  • A clear decision you can defend.
  • The same table works as a revision sheet.
  • It shows trade-off thinking.

⚠️ Problems

  • Real systems might still choose UUIDs for simplicity.
  • Snowflake needs operational care.
  • Requirements can change the answer.

Interview questions and answers

Which ID generation approach would you choose and why?
Snowflake, because it is unique, 64-bit, sortable by time, decentralized and fast. The others fail at least one requirement.
When would a UUID be fine?
When ordering and size do not matter, for example for random tokens or when IDs are created on offline clients.
Cross question: How would the answer change if IDs did not need to be time-ordered?
UUIDs or a simple ticket server with batching become more attractive because the extra complexity of timestamps is not needed.
Cross question: What would you monitor?
Clock drift, the rate of IDs per machine, sequence exhaustion within a millisecond, and the health of each generator.
